title: When things break: handling an incident calmly
summary: A simple, repeatable order for the bad day: confirm, stop the damage with a rollback or a kill switch, tell people, fix it properly, and learn from it without blame.
youWillLearn: Why you stop the damage first and look for the cause second
How a rollback and a kill switch buy you calm time
What to tell users and clients while it is still broken
How to run a short, blameless review so it does not happen again

glossary.incident: Any unplanned problem that hurts users right now, like an outage, a broken feature or leaked data.
glossary.severity: How bad an incident is, usually ranked: everyone blocked, some users blocked, or minor annoyance.
glossary.mitigate: Reduce the harm quickly, even before you know the cause. Rolling back is the classic example.
glossary.rollback: Putting the previous working version of the app back live, without building anything new.
glossary.kill switch: A setting that turns one feature off instantly, without a deploy, while the rest of the app keeps working.
glossary.feature flag: An on/off setting checked by the code at runtime, so a feature can be enabled or disabled without changing code.
glossary.status page: A public page that tells users what is broken and when the next update will come.
glossary.root cause: The underlying reason an incident happened, as opposed to the visible symptom.
glossary.postmortem: A short written review after an incident: what happened, why, and what will change. Blameless means it looks at systems, not at people.

steps.title: Friday, 18:40, the phone buzzes
body: Sentry alert: AI summary errors, hundreds of users, starting right after the 18:25 deploy. Maya's heart rate jumps.
She opens the code and starts changing things directly on main. Three quick fixes in ten minutes. The third one breaks login as well. Panic turned one broken feature into a broken app.

scene.caption: Rushed fixes pushed straight to main make a small outage bigger.

steps.title: A fixed order for bad days
body: Calm comes from having a plan before you need it. Every incident follows the same order.
Confirm what is broken. Stop the damage. Tell people. Fix the cause properly. Learn from it. The key move: stopping the damage comes before understanding it.

callout.text: First aid. You stop the bleeding before you ask how the accident happened. The diagnosis comes later, in a calmer room.

scene.caption: Five steps, always in this order. Stopping the damage comes before the fix.

steps.title: Confirm: what broke, for whom, since when
body: Take two minutes to look before you act. Is it real? Which feature? How many users? When did it start, and what changed right before? A deploy, a config change, a provider outage?
Then give it a severity. Everyone blocked from their notes is top severity. Summaries failing but notes working is serious, not a catastrophe.

callout.text: Check your providers' status pages too. If the Claude API or Supabase is having an outage, your fix is a clear error message and patience, not a code change.

scene.caption: Confirm first: errors started at 18:25, the minute of the last deploy.

steps.title: Stop the damage: roll back
body: The errors started with the 18:25 deploy, so the fastest way to mitigate is to put the 17:10 version back live. That is a rollback.
On Vercel, every deployment is kept. Instant Rollback points the domain back at an older one in seconds, no build needed. Users get a working app while you investigate at your own pace.

callout.text: The bad code is still on main. Revert it there too (lesson 1). Vercel also stops auto-promoting new production deploys after an Instant Rollback, so your fix goes live only when you promote it.

scene.caption: The domain points back at the last good deployment. Users are fine again.

steps.title: Or switch off only one feature
body: Sometimes rolling back is not an option: the bug is old, or the Claude API itself is failing. Then turn off only the broken part with a kill switch.
It is a feature flag the code checks on every request. Summaries pause with a friendly message, and notes keep working.

code.caption: Store the flag in the database or a flag service. On Vercel, changing an env var only takes effect after a redeploy.

scene.caption: One switch turns off summaries. The rest of Notely keeps running.

steps.title: Tell people early, then on a schedule
body: Silence feels worse than bad news. Post a short update as soon as you have confirmed the problem, on a status page or in the app, and tell the client directly.
Say what is affected, what is safe, what you are doing, and when the next update comes. Then keep that promise, even if the update is "still working on it".

code.code:
AI summaries are failing for most users since 18:25.
Your notes are safe and the rest of Notely works.
We have paused summaries and are working on a fix.
Next update by 19:30.
code.caption: Four sentences: what broke, what is safe, what you are doing, when you will speak again.

scene.caption: While the fix is in progress, users and the client hear from Maya first.

steps.title: Fix it properly, on a branch
body: Now there is time. Find the root cause, not only the symptom. The 18:25 deploy renamed a field, and the summary route still read the old name.
Fix it the normal way: a branch, a test that reproduces the bug (lesson 3), a pull request, a preview. Then turn summaries back on and watch Sentry for a few minutes.

callout.text: Paste the full stack trace and the time it started. Ask Claude Code to explain the cause before it changes code. Ask for the smallest fix, on a branch, with a test that failed before and passes after. Refuse pushes to main and unrelated cleanup during an incident.

scene.caption: The real fix goes through the normal route: branch, test, PR, merge.

steps.title: A rollback does not roll back data
body: Rolling back swaps the code, not the database. If the bad deploy ran a migration, or wrote broken rows for twenty minutes, those are still there.
The old code may even crash on the new database shape. That is why migrations should be additive (add a column, stop using the old one later) and why the data needs checking after every incident.

callout.text: If a migration dropped or renamed a column, a rollback can make things worse. That is the case for point-in-time recovery from lesson 5, so know where your backups are before the bad day.

scene.caption: The code went back to 17:10. The database did not.

steps.title: Learn: a blameless postmortem
body: Within a few days, write a one-page postmortem: timeline, impact, root cause, what helped, and two or three concrete changes.
Blameless means asking "what let this through?", not "who did it?". Here: no test covered the summary route, and the rename shipped in one step. Both become tasks.

callout.text: For client work, a calm postmortem is a trust builder. Clients forgive outages. They do not forgive silence or the same outage twice.

scene.caption: The review turns one bad evening into lasting fixes.

steps.title: Recap: stop, tell, fix, learn
body: When something breaks, follow the order: confirm, stop the damage, tell people, fix, learn. Roll back or flip a kill switch first; investigate once users are safe.
Remember that code rolls back but data does not. Fix through the normal branch and PR route, and write a short, blameless review.

quiz.question: Errors spiked right after a deploy 15 minutes ago. You think you know which line is wrong. What do you do first?

options.text: Push a fix to main right away, since you know the line.
options.why: You think you know. If you are wrong, you have added a second untested change to a live incident.

options.text: Roll back to the previous deployment, then fix it on a branch.
options.why: Rollback restores users in seconds and gives you calm time. The fix then goes through tests and a preview like any other change.

options.text: Wait to see if the errors stop on their own.
options.why: Errors that start right after a deploy are almost always caused by it. Waiting only extends the outage.

quiz.question: The Claude API is having an outage. Summaries fail, but the rest of Notely works. What is the best move?

options.text: Roll back to last week's deployment.
options.why: Your code did not change; the provider is down. An older version calls the same failing API.

options.text: Ask Claude Code to rewrite the summary route.
options.why: Nothing is wrong with your code. Rewriting it during an outage adds risk and fixes nothing.

options.text: Turn summaries off with a kill switch, show a friendly message, post a status update.
options.why: You cannot fix their outage. You can make your app fail gracefully and keep users informed until it recovers.

quiz.question: You rolled back a deploy that also ran a migration renaming notes.body to notes.content. The app still crashes. Why?

options.text: The rollback did not finish. Try it again.
options.why: The rollback worked. It only changes code.

options.text: The old code expects body, but the database now has content.
options.why: Rollbacks swap code, never data. Renames should happen in steps (add new column, copy, switch code, drop old later) so old and new code both work.

options.text: Vercel's cache is serving the new code.
options.why: Instant Rollback switches the deployment directly. The mismatch is between code and database.

takeaways: Follow one order every time: confirm, stop the damage, tell people, fix, learn.
Mitigate before you investigate: a rollback or a kill switch buys calm time.
Post early updates with a promised time for the next one. Silence is worse than bad news.
Rollbacks swap code, not data. Keep migrations additive so old code still works.
Write a short, blameless postmortem with two or three concrete changes.
